newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA sees scope for faster Australian growth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA sees scope for faster Australian growth.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia, in announcing a 0.5 percentage point cut in official cash interest rates to 5.0 percent, said the cut was based on the current inflation outlook and that there was scope for faster growth in output and employment.

It said prices and wages confirmed an absence of inflationary pressures and upward pressure on wages were now subsiding. The central bank saw underlying inflation remaining below two percent into 1998.

"This change, like the four previous reductions in interest rates over the past year, is based on the improving picture for Australia's medium term inflation performance, which opens up scope for faster growth in output and employment," the bank said in a statement announcing the cut.
"Recent good news on prices and wages confirms the absence of inflationary pressures in most segments of the Australian economy," the bank said.

The Reserve Bank pointed to the underlying rate of inflation in the year to the June quarter of 1.7 percent in making its decision. "Measures of inflation at the producer level, and indications of price increases from the range of business surveys, generally confirm this picture," the Reserve Bank said.
Traded goods prices had fallen over the past year and inflationary pressures had also been declining, it said.
"Recent data on average earnings suggest that the upward pressures on wages that were still being felt in 1996 are now subsiding," the RBA said.

Some of this easing in prices and wages no doubt reflected the lagged effect of slower growth last year, but it was also clear that inflationary expectations had taken a further step down, the bank said. Economic growth had been picking up in 1997, but remained moderate, it said.

"Unemployment has been flat over the past year and utilisation of capital in goods-producing industries is well down on peak levels. As a result, there appears to be relatively little risk of encountering capacity constraints over the next year or two, even if growth was stronger than expected," it said.
Monetary policy could not fine-tune the cycle or manufacture sustained high rates of real growth, the bank said.
"Given the current conjecture, however, monetary policy should not stand in the way of a period of stronger growth that can be accommodated without breaching the inflation objective."
"Indeed, one attraction of an inflation targeting regime is that it requires the central bank to re-assess policy when the forecast profile of inflation is below the objective."
"In reaching a decision, the bank has also had to be mindful of the fact that earlier interest rate reductions are still working their way through the economy."
"Its judgment, however, is that the balance of risks at this time is such as to favour this further easing of monetary policy."
The bank said the crucial test for monetary policy was to have the setting that would best contribute to low inflation and economic growth in the long run.
Many in the financial markets seemed devoted to picking the exact day when a change in monetary policy would occur, the bank said.
"This would be made easier if the bank were to follow a rule such as changing monetary policy on the day following the Board meeting," it said.

"Despite its simplicity, this has never become standard practice because of its lack of flexibility," it said, noting only eight of the 22 changes made since 1990 have occurred on the day following the board meeting.
This time, the good consumer price index (CPI) and wages data led to a presumption of a further reduction in interest rates, the Reserve Bank said.
"As a result, the bank decided to confer, ahead of the routine meeting with board members to seek their views on the stance and timing of policy."
Today's announcement reflected that consultation.

"With the Board agreed on the need for a half-point reduction in interest rates, and with this fully factored into financial prices, there seemed to be no point in delaying the implementation for another week."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
